lead: Raw owning pointers are fragile — a single early `return` can bypass `delete` and silently leak memory. Chapter 22 shows how RAII wraps resources inside objects whose destructors make cleanup automatic, then teaches *move semantics*: the language mechanism that lets ownership transfer cheaply instead of copying. By the end you will confidently choose between `std::unique_ptr` and `std::shared_ptr`, write correct move constructors and move assignment operators, and understand exactly when and why to write `std::move`.

aids.title: Named rvalue-ref variables are still lvalues
aids.md: A variable declared `std::string&& value` has type *rvalue reference to string*, but the *expression* `value` is a named variable — and named variables are always lvalues. Think of it this way: the `&&` describes what kind of thing `value` was bound from, not what it is now. This is why you must write `std::move(value)` inside the function body to forward it as an rvalue; writing `value` alone silently routes to the lvalue overload (or causes a compile error when the destination only accepts rvalues).

aids.title: Move assignment: release first, then steal
aids.md: Unlike a move *constructor*, move *assignment* lands in an object that already owns a resource. The first real step — after the self-assignment guard — is `delete[] m_data` (or the equivalent for your resource). Skipping this step leaks whatever the destination was holding. The order is: (1) guard self-assignment, (2) release destination's current resource, (3) copy the pointer values from the source, (4) zero the source so its destructor is harmless.

aids.title: std::move is a cast, not a move
aids.md: `std::move(x)` does not move anything by itself — it is a cast that says "treat `x` as something that may be moved from." The *actual transfer* of data happens only if the constructor or assignment operator that receives the result is a move operation. If no move operation exists, the compiler falls back to the copy operation instead. The practical consequence: writing `std::move(x)` and then reading `x` afterward is unsafe only when the move operation actually ran; but since you cannot always tell from a glance, treat any moved-from value as consumed and do not rely on its old contents.

aids.title: One raw pointer, two shared_ptrs — the silent double-delete
aids.md: If you construct two `std::shared_ptr` objects independently from the same raw pointer, each creates its *own* control block and each thinks it is the sole owner. The reference count in each block reaches zero separately, causing the pointed-at object to be deleted twice — undefined behavior. The fix is to call `std::make_shared` once and then *copy* the resulting `shared_ptr` to share ownership; all copies point at the same control block, so the count stays accurate.

xrefs.md: The `new`/`delete` and `new[]`/`delete[]` mechanics that smart pointers wrap — and the leak patterns they prevent — were introduced in Chapter 19.
The shallow-copy trap shown here is the same double-delete hazard introduced with custom copy constructors and operator overloading in Chapter 21.

The Rule of Five extends the Rule of Three (destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment) that was introduced in Chapter 21; move constructors and move assignment operators are the two members added when move semantics enter the picture.
